title: The Courtroom Escape Hatches Sovereign Citizens Swear By

sentences.text: A man on trial in Ohio told the court he reserved his rights "per UCC 1-308 without prejudice", and then added, "I give the Court no consent".

assertions.text: In State v. Smith, an Ohio defendant told the court he reserved his rights "per UCC 1-308 without prejudice".

quote.text: per UCC 1-308 without prejudice

assertions.text: The same defendant told the court "I give the Court no consent".

quote.text: I give the Court no consent

sentences.note: The trial transcript quoted in State v. Smith (Ohio App. 2024); the outcome is held back for question 1.

sentences.text: He believed those words, said in the right place, would leave the judge with no power over him.
sentences.note: Framing of what the defendant intended; no fact beyond the quoted words.

sentences.text: Is there anything you can say, sign or point to that takes you out of a court's jurisdiction?
The people who sell this idea offer a whole kit: a code to write under your signature, a fringe on the courtroom flag, an old act of Congress, and the theory that every law is just a contract.
sentences.note: Lists the tricks the question section takes one by one; each is attributed and judged there.

sentences.text: Each one leans on something real, so we can look at what it rests on, and then read what courts did when someone tried it.

sections.name: question-1
sections.title: Can you sign, say or point your way out of a court's power?

sentences.text: The kit starts with consent. A channel called Out of Babylon puts it plainly: "there are various jurisdictions that do not have jurisdiction over you unless you grant them that jurisdiction".

assertions.text: Out of Babylon says "there are various jurisdictions that do not have jurisdiction over you unless you grant them that jurisdiction".

quote.text: there are various jurisdictions that do not have jurisdiction over you unless you grant them that jurisdiction
quote.speaker: Out of Babylon

sentences.text: And the way to withhold that consent, according to The Grown Academy, is to "write UCC 1-308 next to your signature All Rights Reserved".

assertions.text: The Grown Academy tells viewers to "write UCC 1-308 next to your signature All Rights Reserved".

quote.text: write UCC 1-308 next to your signature All Rights Reserved
quote.speaker: The Grown Academy

sentences.text: So what does that code section actually say?

It is part of the Uniform Commercial Code, and it says a party that "performs, promises performance, or assents to performance" while explicitly reserving its rights does not lose them; words like "without prejudice" or "under protest" are enough.

assertions.text: UCC 1-308 says a party that "performs, promises performance, or assents to performance" with an explicit reservation of rights does not prejudice the rights reserved, and "without prejudice" or "under protest" suffice.

quote.text: performs, promises performance, or assents to performance

sentences.text: The official comment gives its purpose: the continuation of performance "along the lines contemplated by the contract despite a pending dispute".

assertions.text: The official comment says UCC 1-308 provides for the continuation of performance "along the lines contemplated by the contract despite a pending dispute".

quote.text: along the lines contemplated by the contract despite a pending dispute

sentences.text: Picture a shop that keeps accepting a supplier's deliveries while it argues about the bill, and doesn't want accepting them to count as dropping the argument.
sentences.note: An illustration of the mercantile device the official comment describes (going ahead with delivery or acceptance under protest); no figure.

sentences.text: That is the whole job of the section: it is about performing a commercial contract, and it says nothing about courts, police or criminal charges.

assertions.text: UCC 1-308 concerns performance of a commercial contract during a dispute and does not address courts or criminal law.

sentences.text: And the man in Ohio? He was found guilty of all four charges, and the appeals court noted that "Any arguments related to the UCC are unavailing".

assertions.text: In State v. Smith the defendant was found guilty of all 4 charges, and the court noted "Any arguments related to the UCC are unavailing".

quote.text: Any arguments related to the UCC are unavailing

sentences.text: Withholding consent out loud fares no better than writing it down.
In United States v. Benabe, a federal appeals court wrote that whatever status a person claims, "that person is not beyond the jurisdiction of the courts".

assertions.text: United States v. Benabe held that regardless of claimed status, "that person is not beyond the jurisdiction of the courts".

quote.text: that person is not beyond the jurisdiction of the courts
quote.speaker: United States v. Benabe

sentences.text: It added that such theories "should be rejected summarily, however they are presented".

assertions.text: The Benabe court said these theories "should be rejected summarily, however they are presented".

quote.text: should be rejected summarily, however they are presented

sentences.text: Courts in New Zealand heard the same argument from people who said a court's authority depended on their consent, and all three lost; the researchers who reviewed those cases put the problem simply: "no one needs to explicitly and affirmatively consent to the authority of a jurisdiction to be subject to it".

assertions.text: Hobbs, Young and McIntyre report 3 claimants who treated the court's authority as a matter of their consent; all 3 were unsuccessful.
Hobbs, Young and McIntyre write that "no one needs to explicitly and affirmatively consent to the authority of a jurisdiction to be subject to it".

quote.text: no one needs to explicitly and affirmatively consent to the authority of a jurisdiction to be subject to it

sentences.note: The verdict note places the three cases in New Zealand courts.

sentences.text: Then there is the flag.
A letter in the Mountain Democrat newspaper states the belief in one line: "The fringe denotes Admiralty law's jurisdiction".

assertions.text: A letter in the Mountain Democrat says "The fringe denotes Admiralty law's jurisdiction".

quote.text: The fringe denotes Admiralty law's jurisdiction
quote.speaker: Mountain Democrat

sentences.text: A federal court, noting that other courts had already called the argument frivolous, decided to examine the law of the flag "in the interest of killing this argument for good".

assertions.text: In McCann v. Greenway the court examined the law of the flag "in the interest of killing this argument for good", noting other courts had called it frivolous.

quote.text: in the interest of killing this argument for good

sentences.text: It found that the Army's own Adjutant General had written that a fringe "is not considered to be a part of the flag, and it is without heraldic significance".

assertions.text: McCann v. Greenway quotes the Adjutant General of the Army: a fringe "is not considered to be a part of the flag, and it is without heraldic significance".

quote.text: is not considered to be a part of the flag, and it is without heraldic significance
quote.speaker: Adjutant General

sentences.text: Then it said what decides the question: "Jurisdiction is a matter of law, statute, and constitution, not a child's game wherein one's power is magnified or diminished by the display of some magic talisman".

assertions.text: McCann v. Greenway: "Jurisdiction is a matter of law, statute, and constitution, not a child's game wherein one's power is magnified or diminished by the display of some magic talisman".

quote.text: Jurisdiction is a matter of law, statute, and constitution, not a child's game wherein one's power is magnified or diminished by the display of some magic talisman

sentences.text: The next trick goes bigger: it says the whole country was quietly turned into a company.
The channel SYDLIS says "the act of 1871 that is exactly what changed america from a constitutional republic to a corporation".

assertions.text: SYDLIS says "the act of 1871 that is exactly what changed america from a constitutional republic to a corporation".

quote.text: the act of 1871 that is exactly what changed america from a constitutional republic to a corporation
quote.speaker: SYDLIS

sentences.text: The act of 1871 is real, and the Supreme Court later described what it did: it made the District of Columbia "a body corporate for municipal purposes", a local government that could make contracts, sue and be sued, and look after its streets.

assertions.text: The Supreme Court in Metropolitan R. Co. v. District of Columbia described the act of 1871 as constituting the District of Columbia "a body corporate for municipal purposes", with power to make contracts and sue and be sued, and a board of public works over its streets.

quote.text: a body corporate for municipal purposes

sentences.text: The Court called the District "a mere municipal corporation", and said the sovereign power over it was lodged "in the government of the United States".

assertions.text: The Court held the District's character is that of "a mere municipal corporation".

quote.text: a mere municipal corporation

assertions.text: The Court said the sovereign power over the District is lodged "in the government of the United States".

quote.text: in the government of the United States

sentences.text: And the government that the 1871 act set up did not even last: an act of 1874 abolished it.

assertions.text: The District government established by the act of 1871 was abolished by an act passed in 1874.

sentences.text: The last item in the kit is the broadest.
Americans In Action says that "these codes and statutes are only the bylaws of the corporation", rules that, it says, do not bind state nationals.

assertions.text: Americans In Action says "these codes and statutes are only the bylaws of the corporation".

quote.text: these codes and statutes are only the bylaws of the corporation
quote.speaker: Americans In Action

sentences.note: The source context says state nationals "are not obligated by corporate government rules"; the clause after the quote paraphrases that.

sentences.text: In Bey v. Indiana, a man argued that Indiana could not tax him without a contract between them, and the federal appeals court answered: "We have repeatedly rejected such claims".

assertions.text: In Bey v. Indiana the plaintiff argued he could not be taxed by Indiana absent a contract; the Seventh Circuit wrote "We have repeatedly rejected such claims".

quote.text: We have repeatedly rejected such claims
quote.speaker: Bey v. Indiana

sentences.text: In New Zealand, a self-described freeman said he had never consented to the Land Transport Act and so was not bound by it; the court struck out his claim as an abuse of process.

assertions.text: In James v The Corporation New Zealand Police, a freeman-on-the-land who said he had not consented to the Land Transport Act had his claim struck out as an abuse of process.

sentences.text: The reason is simple: "Everyone who operates a vehicle on public roads must comply with legislation regulating the operation of vehicles".

assertions.text: Hobbs, Young and McIntyre, on that case: "Everyone who operates a vehicle on public roads must comply with legislation regulating the operation of vehicles".

quote.text: Everyone who operates a vehicle on public roads must comply with legislation regulating the operation of vehicles

sentences.text: So the answer to the first question is no: courts in the United States, Canada and New Zealand have rejected the idea that their power depends on your consent.

assertions.text: Courts in the United States, Canada and New Zealand have rejected the argument that a court has no jurisdiction without the person's consent.

sentences.text: Researchers who followed these arguments to the Supreme Court of Canada found that it has never granted one of them leave to appeal, and their verdict is blunt: "These ideas are pseudolaw, and devoid of merit".

assertions.text: Netolitzky and Warman report that to date no pseudolaw-based appeal has been granted leave by the Supreme Court of Canada, and write "These ideas are pseudolaw, and devoid of merit".

quote.text: These ideas are pseudolaw, and devoid of merit

qualifications: This is the Canadian record; s36 says the US record is case law, not a count; the tax-only IRS verdict is not cited here.

sentences.note: Uses "never granted" from "To date no OPCA-based appeal has been granted leave".

sentences.text: A review of cases in Australia and New Zealand reached the same place: "No courts accept these arguments, and no courts absolve the claimant (or defendant) from their legal obligations and responsibilities".

assertions.text: Hobbs, Young and McIntyre write "No courts accept these arguments, and no courts absolve the claimant (or defendant) from their legal obligations and responsibilities".

quote.text: No courts accept these arguments, and no courts absolve the claimant (or defendant) from their legal obligations and responsibilities

qualifications: The sentence names Australia and New Zealand as the review's scope; s36 gives the narrower US record.

sentences.text: For the United States, the evidence here has no count like that; what it has is a run of rulings, and the Ohio appeals court summed them up by saying the claims "continue to make their way to court and fail".

assertions.text: State v. Smith says this court and many others have repeatedly rejected such claims, which "continue to make their way to court and fail".

quote.text: continue to make their way to court and fail

qualifications: The sentence scopes the absence of a count to this evidence and says the US evidence is a run of rulings.

sentences.text: If nothing you say, sign or point to removes a court's power, the promoters' next offer is to change who you are.

sections.name: question-2
sections.title: Can declaring a new status put you outside the law?

sentences.text: A channel called Sovereign National describes ordinary citizenship as the thing "which forces you into their statutes and codes and bylaws and we are not part of that".

assertions.text: Sovereign National says citizenship is what "which forces you into their statutes and codes and bylaws and we are not part of that".

quote.text: which forces you into their statutes and codes and bylaws and we are not part of that
quote.speaker: Sovereign National

sentences.text: Some sellers promise that the paperwork works at the roadside too: SPC University tells viewers that "when the officer runs your id he or she will see your status and has to let you go".

assertions.text: SPC University says "when the officer runs your id he or she will see your status and has to let you go".

quote.text: when the officer runs your id he or she will see your status and has to let you go
quote.speaker: SPC University

sentences.text: So what is a national, in the law itself?
Federal statute defines a national of the United States as "a citizen of the United States", or a person who is not a citizen but owes the country permanent allegiance.

assertions.text: By statute, a national of the United States means "a citizen of the United States", or a non-citizen who owes permanent allegiance to the United States.

quote.text: a citizen of the United States

qualifications: These are definitions from statute; s43 carries the tax-only limit of the court rulings on state citizenship and s53 says state jurisdiction is untested.

sentences.text: So every citizen is already a national, and the non-citizen kind comes from the circumstances of birth, such as being born in an outlying possession of the United States, not from a form you file.

assertions.text: Every US citizen is a national of the United States, and non-citizen national status comes at birth, for example from birth in an outlying possession, not from a declaration.
qualifications: These are definitions from statute; s43 carries the tax-only limit of the court rulings on state citizenship and s53 says state jurisdiction is untested.

sentences.text: Federal appeals courts, in tax cases, have also rejected the related claim that being a citizen of a state rather than of the United States puts a person beyond the federal courts; one called it "barely worth a footnote".

assertions.text: In tax cases, federal circuits rejected claims that being a citizen of a state rather than the United States puts a person beyond federal court jurisdiction; the Second Circuit called the argument "barely worth a footnote".

quote.text: barely worth a footnote

qualifications: The sentence says these are tax cases in federal court; s53 adds that state jurisdiction is not tested by them.

sentences.text: The Moorish version leans on old treaties instead, and the Institute for Strategic Dialogue explains how: "Moorish sovereigns cite that treaty to claim that Moors in the US have sovereign status, meaning they would be exempt from normal laws".

assertions.text: The Institute for Strategic Dialogue explains "Moorish sovereigns cite that treaty to claim that Moors in the US have sovereign status, meaning they would be exempt from normal laws".

quote.text: Moorish sovereigns cite that treaty to claim that Moors in the US have sovereign status, meaning they would be exempt from normal laws
quote.speaker: Institute for Strategic Dialogue

sentences.text: In Bey v. Indiana, the man who argued that being a Moor made him a sovereign citizen wanted an $11.5 billion refund from the State of Indiana.

assertions.text: In Bey v. Indiana, the plaintiff, who said being a Moor made him a sovereign citizen, sought an $11.5 billion refund from the State of Indiana.

sentences.text: The court said the treaty argument is made "without any basis in fact", and that Bey "is a U.S. citizen and therefore unlike foreign diplomats has no immunity from U.S. law".

assertions.text: The Seventh Circuit said the argument that eighteenth-century treaties remove US jurisdiction over Moors is made "without any basis in fact".

quote.text: without any basis in fact

assertions.text: The Seventh Circuit said Bey "is a U.S. citizen and therefore unlike foreign diplomats has no immunity from U.S. law".

quote.text: is a U.S. citizen and therefore unlike foreign diplomats has no immunity from U.S. law

sentences.text: The oldest-sounding version reaches back to the common law, and the National Liberty Alliance teaches that "the un-codified common law is the superior law of the people and the codified civil law is the special or inferior law of the government".

assertions.text: The National Liberty Alliance says "the un-codified common law is the superior law of the people and the codified civil law is the special or inferior law of the government".

quote.text: the un-codified common law is the superior law of the people and the codified civil law is the special or inferior law of the government
quote.speaker: National Liberty Alliance

sentences.text: As for Magna Carta, it had been repealed by 1969 except for three provisions.

assertions.text: By 1969, the whole of Magna Carta save 3 provisions had been repealed.

sentences.text: As early as 1905, the High Court of Australia said the claim that a law is invalid because it does not conform to Magna Carta "is not one for serious refutation".

assertions.text: In 1905 the High Court of Australia said the contention that a Commonwealth law is invalid for nonconformity with Magna Carta "is not one for serious refutation".

quote.text: is not one for serious refutation

sentences.text: And the Supreme Court of Canada has refused to hear appeals built on Magna Carta and historical English common law, which the researchers read as a quiet rejection of both.

assertions.text: Netolitzky and Warman report that the Supreme Court of Canada denied leave in applications relying on Magna Carta and historical English common law, implicitly rejecting them.

sentences.text: On the papers that are meant to stop police, the evidence is thin: one FBI bulletin reports that three people in Kansas City were convicted for selling "sovereign status" ID cards, at $450 to $2,000 each, that promised immunity from stops and arrests, and it records the sellers' convictions, not what happened to buyers at a stop.

assertions.text: The FBI Law Enforcement Bulletin reports that 3 sovereign-citizen extremists in Kansas City were convicted for selling identification cards, at $450 to $2,000, that supposedly gave immunity from stops and arrests.
qualifications: The sentence calls the evidence thin, names it as one bulletin, and says it records the sellers' convictions, not what happened to holders at stops.

sentences.text: So the answer to the second question is no as well: no court in this evidence has accepted a declared status, whether state national, Moor or free man under the common law.

assertions.text: Courts have rejected the claim that being a citizen of a state rather than of the United States removes federal court jurisdiction.
qualifications: s43 says these are tax prosecutions; s53 says what they leave untested.

assertions.text: A self-described Moor has no immunity from US law.
Courts have rejected the claim that Magna Carta or historical common law overrides statutes.

sentences.text: The parts settled less directly are narrow: the federal rulings on state citizenship come from tax cases, so a state court's reach is not what they tested, and the stop question rests on the bulletin above.

assertions.text: The federal rulings rejecting state-citizen status are from tax cases, so state jurisdiction is not covered.
qualifications: This sentence is the qualification itself.

assertions.text: The evidence on protection at stops is the one FBI report about sellers of immunity cards being convicted.
qualifications: This sentence is the qualification itself.

sentences.note: The only limits that apply to the whole second answer; they point back to s43 and s51 in words.

sentences.text: Both answers come down to the same thing: a court gets its power from the law, not from what you write under your name, what hangs on its wall, or what you declare yourself to be.

assertions.text: Jurisdiction is a matter of law, statute and constitution, not of displayed symbols.
Regardless of claimed status, a person is not beyond the jurisdiction of the courts.

sentences.text: So if someone offers you a form, a code to write by your signature, or a card for the glovebox, ask them for one ruling where it worked.
The rulings where it was tried are public, and they are the place to look before you sign anything.
